papers.title: Retweeting patterns reveal partisan asymmetries in information sharing and signal state-level electoral outcomes in the 2020 US presidential election
papers.abstract: As social media has become a primary source of political information, concerns are growing that online information consumption may intensify political polarization and reshape democratic processes. Yet how large-scale online information consumption organizes polarized political ecosystems and relates to offline voting remains unclear. Here we reconstruct partisan information ecosystems from more than 500 million tweets generated during the 2020 US presidential election, integrating information diffusion across media outlets, influencers, and social peers. Contrary to the conventional expectation that broader information exposure promotes moderation, we find that retweeting a wider range of political information is associated with stronger political polarization. We further show systematic asymmetries in political information ecosystems: the Republican ecosystem is highly concentrated and ideologically biased, whereas the Democratic ecosystem is more dispersed and primarily organized around relatively moderate left-leaning sources. Finally, we demonstrate that several shared retweeting signatures robustly map onto state-level electoral outcomes despite cross-state heterogeneity. Our findings reveal asymmetric political information ecosystems as a key organizing principle of online political communication and identify collective retweeting patterns as a scalable signal of real-world voting behaviours.

papers.title: Predictability of Collective Behavior in Networks of LLM Agents
papers.abstract: As AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) increasingly interact at scale, anticipating their collective behavior becomes necessary. Unlike humans, individual LLM agents can be probed in {controlled scenarios}; however, the predictability of their collective outcomes hinges on what such measurements capture. We study information cascades on networks of LLM agents that decide whether to share a post given how many of their contacts have shared it. At the same fraction of sharing contacts, an agent's response depends on how many contacts it has and on the post. Responses that ignore the number of contacts mispredict the cascades, increasingly on heterogeneous networks, by an error we derive analytically and that network topology alone cannot reveal. Measured in context, the response predicts, through mean-field theory, the cascades of full LLM simulations, tipping points included. Anticipating the collective behavior of AI agents thus requires evaluating them in their local network context.
papers.tldr_zh: 研究LLM智能体网络中的信息级联，发现智能体响应依赖联系人数量与帖子内容，忽略联系人数量会误判级联，且异质网络上误差更大。

papers.title: Evidence and measures of the digital usage divide from 40 million Windows devices
papers.abstract: Abstract Digital infrastructure is crucial for economic opportunities, social inclusion, and civic participation, but benefits remain unevenly distributed. Existing measures, such as computer ownership and broadband adoption, do not capture the depth and variety of digital use. We develop measures using Microsoft telemetry collected during operating system updates from 40 million Windows devices in U.S. households. These measures provide greater coverage and granularity than existing commercial or government surveys. Device representations at the ZIP-code level reveal substantial variation in usage, including an urban-rural divide and disparities within narrowly defined Metropolitan Statistical Areas. Income and education correlate with these differences. These effects are large and suggest that digital usage gaps extend beyond the local availability of essential IT infrastructure. The findings call for interventions that complement infrastructure access with support for technology use and skills development. The resulting indices are publicly available to support future research on digital inequality.

papers.title: Continuous modeling of manipulative participation for stance analysis: Online discourse on the 2024 Street Animal Law in Türkiye
papers.abstract: Studies of online political discourse commonly infer public opinion through stance analysis while implicitly assuming that observed user participation is authentic. Meanwhile, studies focusing on detecting manipulative participation are typically modeling it as a binary phenomenon, overlooking the varying degrees to which users may engage in coordinated or inauthentic behavior. This study proposes a continuous modeling approach for manipulative participation and examines its integration with stance analysis. Using online discourse on the 2024 Street Animal Law in Türkiye as a case study, we collected a dataset comprising 7,320,574 tweets from 537,994 users. From this corpus, 301 users were selected through a high-information sampling strategy and manually annotated by domain experts using a 10-criterion rubric that yields user-level continuous manipulative participation scores. Evaluation under a unified user-level cross-validation protocol showed that the proposed framework accurately estimates both manipulative participation and user stance, with gradient boosting methods providing the best manipulative participation estimates and BERTurk achieving the highest stance classification performance. External validation on an independently annotated user set demonstrated good generalization performance. The findings support modeling manipulative participation as a continuous construct rather than a binary label, providing a more informative basis for computational analyses of the relationship between manipulative participation and stance in online political discourse.

papers.title: Steering Emergent Behavior in Multi-Agent LLM Systems via Information Networks
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate in groups, each pursuing an individual objective while jointly determining system performance. If an operator controls which agent observes which other agent, but not their payoffs or messages, how should observations be structured to raise collective welfare? We make the information network (who observes whom) a design object, decoupled from the fixed interaction network over which agents act. Ten identical LLM agents play repeated group-decision games; by default each observes only an anonymous summary of the group's previous-round outcome, and a manager with a fixed budget adds directed observation links that reveal peers' past actions. Across 1,080 episodes and six games spanning coordination, anti-coordination, social dilemmas, and discovery, we ask how much information to share and, at a fixed budget, who should observe whom. Disclosure creates behavioral coupling: observation acts as a contagion channel whose welfare effect depends on the alignment between individually attractive behavior and the collective objective. First, the value of information is alignment-contingent: more peer information tends to help or be neutral when individual behavior is aligned with the collective goal, but under free-riding or congestion externalities it amplifies collectively harmful behavior; in a public-goods game the group does best with no information at all. We read this sign separation as a cross-game regularity within one controlled LLM population, not a model-invariant law. Second, at a fixed budget, who observes whom matters primarily when coupling is harmful: a modular "barbell" that lets sub-populations entrench harmful behavior is reliably the worst wiring, reversing the network-reciprocity intuition from human evolutionary game theory. These results argue against a default of full transparency for agent collectives.
papers.tldr_zh: 将信息网络（谁观察谁）作为设计对象，用1080局多智能体LLM博弈实验表明调整观察结构可提升集体福利。

papers.title: The Radicalization Pipeline: Characterizing and Predicting Online Misogyny
papers.abstract: Social media platforms are known to shape and polarize user opinions and, increasingly, facilitate pathways toward ideological extremism. Among these trends, online misogynistic communities associ- ated with the incel (involuntary celibate) ideology have received growing scholarly attention. Previous work has primarily focused on ideological narratives and linguistic content within incel communities them- selves. However, much less is known about how user behaviors evolve over time, particularly before and after their engagement with incel spaces, and whether early signals can anticipate such transitions. In this study, we conduct a longitudinal analysis of Reddit users who participated in the r/incels community on Reddit. Our results show that engagement with the incel community is associated with a substantial in- crease in toxicity in both posts and comments, while hate increases particularly in posts after engagement. These changes extend beyond explicitly ideological communities: users who engage with the r/incels sub- reddit display elevated toxicity and hate speech even in subreddits related to leisure, entertainment, and everyday interests. In parallel, user activity shifts away from recreational and support-oriented communi- ties toward subreddits focused on social issues, indicating a broader reorientation of online participation. Finally, we show that future incel users can be identified with high accuracy prior to engagement using supervised machine learning models trained on linguistic, contextual, and interaction-based features. These findings suggest that online misogynistic radicalization follows detectable behavioral trajectories and diffuses across the broader social media ecosystem.

papers.title: Competing Influence in LLM Populations: Budget Timing and Baseline Drift
papers.abstract: When competing campaigns target a population of large language model (LLM) agents, observed opinion changes may reflect both campaign influence and changes that would occur without intervention. We study how the timing of campaign expenditure and the population's own evolution shape outcomes in a network of persona-conditioned LLM agents that exchange and revise opinions in natural language. A proponent and a challenger are tasked with generating opposing messages under equal delivery budgets, while a separate stance probe measures opinions without influencing the simulation. Across eight claims, we compare single-campaign and competitive conditions against matched no-campaign runs, and evaluate all nine combinations of early, sustained, and late spending on a reference topic. Baseline stance drift varies substantially across claims and, on some, accounts for a sizeable fraction of apparent campaign effects. After accounting for this drift, the direction of observed campaign-associated changes aligns more closely with the claim's epistemic standing than with the campaigner's assigned role. Uninfluenced populations also consistently lose stance diversity, demonstrating that directional opinion change and convergence are distinct phenomena. In networks with two opinion-segregated communities, campaigns primarily reduce differences between communities rather than diversity within them. LLM campaign agents do not always argue for their assigned positions, particularly when these conflict with established evidence. Finally, campaign outcomes depend on the opponent's expenditure schedule: unlike a matched numerical bounded-confidence population receiving interventions at the same times and locations, the LLM population exhibits a payoff structure with no pure-strategy equilibrium.

papers.title: Teamknitt: Configuring, Observing and Intervening in LLM-Agent Teams through the Lens of Dynamical-Systems and Human-Team Theory
papers.abstract: Most frameworks for teams of large language model (LLM) agents fix the team's shape inside the software: who talks to whom, how much is passed along, and what a human can do once a run has started. Human-team research has long asked those questions: where team phenomena live (in members or in their interaction), how team-level properties arise, and what separates what a team does from how a team is. I propose using that theory as the organizing lens for configuring, observing and intervening in LLM-agent teams, without assuming its findings transfer. I introduce teamknitt, a framework and open reference implementation in which a user configures a team of 1-16 AI agents for task completion, solution generation, achieving a goal or a research mission; selects one of fourteen deterministic routing topologies or a custom directed graph; chooses a sharing profile that limits what may travel along permitted routes; and binds sources, representations, work dependencies, handoffs and an expertise directory. The recorded process can be observed through non-system views (member reports and behavior) and system views (distributed problem-solving, differentiated transactive memory, interactive coordination, team dynamics). Interventions are explicit and human-led: reviewed reconfiguration between runs, planned disturbances, and private feedback, pause, resume or stop applied at dependency-wave boundaries, with "queued", "applied", "assembled", "understood" and "improved" kept as separate claims. Emergent states such as trust and shared understanding are declared unmeasured. This is an idea and system-description paper with falsifiable hypotheses on topology, information flow and intervention timing, including whether the fractal scaling of communication output between members, and between members on different models, relates to task and team performance. No comparative result is reported.

papers.title: Who Benefits from Wikipedia's Growth Mentorship? The Role of Newcomer Information Needs
papers.abstract: Evaluations of Wikipedia's programs for new editors usually ask whether a program works on average; we ask which newcomers benefit when their question to a mentor gets a reply. English Wikipedia's Growth mentorship system assigns every new account a volunteer mentor, and about a quarter of the questions newcomers send never get a reply. Using the first questions of 34,073 newcomers (2021 to 2026), we compare newcomers who received a reply with similar newcomers who did not, matched on 164 characteristics recorded before the question (propensity score stratification). (1) Does a reply help newcomers keep editing? Yes, in the short term: in the 14 days after the reply, newcomers who received one were 1.8 percentage points (pp) more likely to edit an article (22% vs. an estimated 20% without a reply) and 1.8pp more likely to edit on two or more days. Later in the first year, the only difference that remains significant after correction for multiple testing is in the share who edit an article at least once between six months and one year after the reply (+1.5pp). (2) Does the effect depend on what the newcomer asked? Yes. We sort questions by Morrison's (1993) information-seeking types, which earlier studies measured mostly through self-reports, using a language model checked against human labels. A reply has significant effects for questions about rules and norms (+3.4pp), questions that show the newcomer's earlier editing (+3.4pp) and specific how-to questions (+2.4pp). For newcomers who do not know what to work on, a reply has no detectable effect, and the effect is 4.2pp smaller than for newcomers with other questions. (3) Which replies are followed by more editing? Among newcomers who received a reply, those whose reply came sooner or stayed closer to the topic of their question edited more.

papers.title: The AI research space shapes country academic performance
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have demonstrated great potential across diverse domains, prompting increasing attention to understanding the AI ecosystem. As knowledge production is often perceived as a process of connecting existing pieces of knowledge, mapping the interconnections of AI knowledge is crucial for unraveling the dynamics of scientific production in AI. However, maps created so far have fallen short of capturing knowledge relatedness, focusing instead on citation relationships between subfields. Here, we build an AI research space by connecting pairs of AI research topics based on their proximity measured through author-topic coupling. Projections of country level performances onto the space reveal that countries exhibit distinct baskets of specializations. We further examine the role of the structure of the AI research space in the scientific development of nations. We find that countries are more likely to gain specialization in topics that have high proximity to already specialized neighbor topics, and that publications whose topics align more with the developed topics in the country are more likely to become high impact. Our results highlight the AI development gaps across nations and the path-dependence in the development induced by the AI research space.
papers.tldr_zh: 用作者-主题耦合构建AI研究空间，发现各国在AI主题空间中呈现不同的专长组合。
